chunks: Simple circuit to switch and regulate a buck. The question: What is a simple circuit to implement the switching?
How can you make it switch with a higher/lower duty cycle based on the feedback voltage?
The simplest regulated buck uses a comparator.
It compares a scaled copy of the output to a reference (a fixed, accurate voltage), and turns the switch on when the output is too low and off when it is too high.
A fixed-frequency version uses a ramp (a voltage that rises steadily each cycle, then resets) and an error amplifier to set how long the switch stays on each cycle.
Both are feedback loops that push the output back toward the target.
This is a thermostat. When the room is too cold, the heater turns on. When it is warm enough, the heater turns off.
A little gap between the on and off temperatures (hysteresis) stops it from flicking on and off nonstop.
The buck does the same with the switch, only thousands of times per second. The fixed-frequency version is more like a heater that is always on for a set share of each minute.
The PFET Q 1 conducts when its gate is pulled below V IN (gate low = ON). The Schottky D 1 carries the inductor current while Q 1 is off.
The divider R 1 over R 2 produces the feedback node. The controller (next figures) drives G and reads FB.
A 12 volts supply is within a typical PFET gate rating ( V GS of 12 to 20 volts), but for higher V IN you'd level-shift the gate.
Comparator: a circuit that outputs high or low depending on which of two voltages is larger. Hysteresis: a small gap between the turn-on and turn-off thresholds.
PWM: pulse width modulation, controlling the on-time share of each fixed period. Error amplifier: an amplifier that measures how far the output is from the target.
Gate driver: a circuit that gives the switch's gate enough drive to switch fast ("Buck IC: integrated vs external parts").
Take a ramp that rises from 0 to 2 volts each cycle. The error amplifier outputs a control voltage of 0. 5 volts. The switch is on while the ramp is below 0.
5 volts, so the duty is 0. 5 over 2 equals 25 % . From a 12 volts input, the ideal output is 12 times 0. 25 equals 3 volts.
If the output sags, the control voltage rises, the duty grows, and the output recovers. That is the whole idea.
"I divide the output to a feedback voltage and use an error amplifier against a reference to make a control voltage.
A comparator compares that voltage to a sawtooth ramp, so duty is control voltage over ramp amplitude, and drives the switch through a gate driver.
If the output rises, the error amp lowers the control voltage and the duty cycle falls.
The even simpler option is a comparator with hysteresis that turns the switch on below the reference and off above it."
